stories.article:
# My first job at the corner drugstore

The summer I turned sixteen, I walked into Miller's Drugstore on Main Street and asked the owner for a job. I had rehearsed the question the whole walk over, and I still stumbled on it.

Mr. Miller hired me to stock shelves and run the register for a dollar and fifteen cents an hour. I learned more in that first year than in any classroom:

- Show up early, every single time.
- If you do not know the answer, ask someone who does.
- Say thank you when a customer is patient with you.

I would not change a thing. That job taught me that work is mostly about trust, and trust is built one small promise at a time.

stories.article:
# Finding love one ordinary day at a time

People ask me for a secret, and I have to tell them there is not one. I met my wife at a church supper in 1968. She was carrying a tray of pies and I was holding the door.

What kept us together for fifty years was not grand gestures. It was:

- Laughing at the same small jokes.
- Saying sorry before the sun went down.
- Choosing each other again on the ordinary days.

If you are looking, stop performing and start paying attention. The right person usually shows up while you are busy being yourself.

stories.article:
# The advice my father gave me

My father was a quiet man, but one afternoon while we were fixing a fence, he told me something I never forgot.

"Measure twice, cut once," he said. "And that goes for words, too."

I did not understand it as a boy. As a man, I have used it a hundred times — before signing a contract, before saying something in anger, before giving up on something worth keeping.

The best advice is rarely complicated. It just arrives at the right moment and waits for you to grow into it.

stories.article:
# A Proud Moment

The proudest moment of my life was probably when my daughter graduated from university. I nearly didn't go. We didn't have much money back then, and I was always worrying about how we'd pay for everything.

My husband Frank worked at a factory, and I worked at a little bakery for a while. Oh, the smell of fresh bread in the morning! When Susan told us she wanted to go to university, I thought, goodness me, how are we going to afford that? We had two children, bills to pay, and the roof was leaking at the time. I remember putting a bucket in the hallway whenever it rained. Frank was always tripping over the thing!

But Susan was determined. She wanted to become a teacher, even when she was little. She used to line up her dolls and pretend to teach them. We took out a loan, and she worked part-time while studying. There were some difficult years, I can tell you. But she never gave up.

On graduation day, there she was, standing in that black gown. When they called her name, I just started crying. Frank handed me his old handkerchief because he knew I'd get emotional. Typical of him, always prepared!

What made me so proud wasn't just that she'd earned a degree. It was knowing how hard she'd worked, and that we'd somehow managed to give her that opportunity, despite not having much ourselves.

Frank passed away twelve years ago, and I wish he could see what Susan has achieved since then. He'd be so proud. Looking back, I don't remember the things we couldn't afford. I remember that day, sitting next to Frank, watching our daughter walk across that stage. Knowing that, together, we'd helped someone we loved get somewhere they wanted to go.

stories.prompt: How did you meet your closest lifelong friend, and what has kept you close?
stories.transcript:
I met my best friend Peter about 55 years ago, when we both started working at a car repair shop. To be honest, I didn't liked him much at first. He was always joking and making fun of me, especially when I made mistakes at work.

One day my car broke down on the way home, and it was raining really bad. Peter happened to drive past and stopped to help me. We spent nearly two hours fixing the car, and we got completely wet. After that we started going for beers after work and became really close friends.

Over the years, we both got married, had children and went through many difficult times. When I lost my job, Peter helped me with groceries, even though he didn't had much money himself. And when my wife passed away six years ago, he visited me almost every Sunday. Sometimes we didn't even talk much, we just watched football together.

I think what kept us close is that we was always there for each other. We don't agree on everything, especially football, because he supports the wrong team, obviously! But a real friendship isn't about agreeing on everything. It's about showing up when someone needs you.

After 55 years, he's more like a brother to me. And I think that's what friendship is really about, being there for each other, even when life gets hard.

stories.article:
# Finding My Path

When I was young, I really didn’t know what I wanted to do with my life. Everyone asked me, "What do you want to become?" and I thought, "How should I know? I was only seventeen!"

My father wanted me to become a mechanic, as he worked with cars and thought it was a good and safe job. But I wasn’t interested in cars. I preferred talking with people and doing things outside. In school, I wasn’t the best student, especially in mathematics. My teacher always said I needed to be more serious about my future.

After school, I took a job in a small shop just to earn some money. I thought I would do it for a few months, but then I met many people and started to enjoy the work. An older man who came in every week once told me, "You are good with people; you should do something with this." I remembered his words for many years.

I ended up working in shops for a long time and eventually became a manager. It wasn’t a big dream I had since childhood; it was more like one thing led to another, and suddenly I was there.

I think young people today worry too much about choosing the perfect path. You don’t need to know everything when you’re young. Just try something, make some mistakes, and see where life takes you. Sometimes the wrong road can lead you to a good place.

stories.article:
# Embracing Uncertainty in Career Choices

When I was young, I didn’t know what I wanted to do in my life. People always asked me, "What do you want to be later?" and I would say, "I don’t know, maybe something good." At 17, I thought it was too young to decide my entire future.

My father wanted me to become a mechanic because he worked with cars and said it was a good job with money and stability. But I didn’t like cars much. I preferred talking with people and hanging out with my friends. In school, I wasn’t a very good student. Math was difficult for me, and my teacher was often angry because I didn’t understand things quickly.

After school, I started working in a small shop. I didn’t choose this job because I loved it; I just needed money. I thought I would stay there only a few months, but I ended up liking the people, and the work wasn’t so bad. An old man came to the shop every week and talked with me a lot. One day, he said, "You are good with people; maybe you can do something with this." I remember that even after many years.

Later, I became a manager in another shop. Sometimes I think, how did this happen? I never planned this life. I just did one thing, then another, and suddenly many years had passed.

I think young people today worry too much about the future. They feel they must know everything and make perfect decisions. But life isn’t like that. You try something; maybe it doesn’t work, then you try something else. I made many mistakes in my life, but that’s also how I learned. You don’t need to have all the answers when you’re young. Just start somewhere and see what happens.

# Nostalgic Days

We had plenty of fun back then. We didn't have smartphones or the internet. If you wanted to see your friends, you just went to their house and knocked on the door. Sometimes they weren't even home, so you walked all the way back again.

When I was about 16, I spent most afternoons playing football with my friends on this little field near our neighborhood. It wasn't a proper field, just some grass and two old jackets for goalposts. We played until it got dark, and my mother would stand outside shouting my name. I always pretended I couldn't hear her.

I remember one summer evening when we sat by the river listening to music on a little radio. One of my friends brought it to the bar, and we tried to guess the songs. If you missed your favorite song, well... you just had to wait until it played again.
